clips.speaker: Wosny Lambre
clips.text: This night went about as poorly as it could have for Jaylen Brown. With the story that came out beforehand and some of the comments he had been making throughout the offseason and early in the season, he was adding fuel to the fire here. For him to have maybe his worst game of the season, just lay a stinker, they have an okay first half, they are hanging around despite not playing their best basketball, they go on this big run to tie the game in the third, and then they just get their ass handed to them the rest of the way. Let's tackle Jaylen Brown's individual night to start. I thought he was pressing a little bit, and I think Boston was just very ready for the game. They felt like the more well-coached team, the more well-prepared team. They knew what Philly was going to try to throw at them, but Jaylen Brown's mode of attack would be they crowded him, they crowded his line of sight. They knew that he would be trying to get downhill and that he would be looking to score on those drives, and they kept throwing extra bodies at him, arms, length at him. He had several turnovers, then he is getting offensive fouls, then he is fouling guys in the back. He was just off of his game.

clips.text: I thought the difference in the game is two offenses in way different forms in terms of their development from one another. That contrast was stark to me. You got the Celtics who have a machine. They have a system. It is tried and true. It is brought championships, it is gotten to conference finals, it is made Joe Mazzulla coach of the year. It is produced. It has done nothing but produce for three, four years now. And yeah, they plug in Paul George, but this guy is a veteran. This guy is a very high IQ player. The requirements of this offense speak directly to his actual strong suits and skill set. And so you see something seamless happening there, whereas in Philly, it is they have way more to figure out and I thought this game was indicative of that truth. 100% agree. I think you have a team that knows its identity and a team that is still figuring it out. And that to me was the big takeaway on both sides. And I think from the Philly side to in terms of being optimistic, like they have been able to win a ton of games so far while they are still finding themselves and they have had a difficult schedule. They have played the Knicks a couple times, the Pistons a couple times, now the Celtics, the Pacers, so like they have had a really difficult schedule. I know by record the Knicks and the Cavs aren't quite what we expected them to be, but those are still good teams.

He goes, after we won games, I think two, five and six, we beat them in six, he goes, they're just better than us. They're playing better than us. That's what Al Attles of the Warriors said after we beat them. He goes, they're just playing better than us.

clips.speaker: Alvan Adams
clips.text: One of my jobs was to be the purchasing agent for all FF&E, all furnishings, fixtures and equipment. One of the things I investigated real closely were basketball standards. There was a company out of Oregon and they had a new goal that they were selling in Europe and the Blazers used at their training camp. In the old days, the support, because I was watching some old video of Dick Van Arsdale getting smashed by Wilton Chamberlain into the old support of just some metal poles crisscrossed and it's only four feet beyond the end the baseline. These new units sat about two feet further back. So I figured it was a safer distance. But I was worried about the longer lever arm. So when Will goes up and dunks it or Mark West goes up and dunks it, how long does it do that before it restores to its quiet position? I decided to go ahead and buy those.
clips.news_angle: Alvan Adams on selecting new basketball standards for the arena

clips.pull_quote: These new units sat about two feet further back. So I figured it was a safer distance.

clips.speaker: Alvan Adams
clips.text: Our first nationally televised game in this building, us playing Orlando and this new big Shaquille O'Neal, and he didn't even swing on or do a chin up. It was late in the second quarter, he grabbed it and let go and the whole thing quietly went back to its restored position. The NBA people were here, the commissioner was here, the guy I called about the goals, I saw him at halftime. He looked at me and he goes, Alvan, I said, I'm fired. I'm fired. Luckily, at the time the league only required you have a spare backboard because of Darryl Dawkins and those guys used to shout about. We had luckily the old two units from the Coliseum. So we were able to get them out, wipe them down with some paper towels and get it out there and finish the game.

clips.text: The win that I'll point the most to throughout this eight-game streak is the Lakers. I think it was really big for us to get that win. Obviously, it was an NBA Cup game, which is always a little more exciting. But even aside from it being an NBA Cup game, that's a team that we played the first game of the season, and we did not look very good. So to come back and play them in game six of the season, after we've kind of gotten our foot in a little bit, that's the win I would point at the most because we were down big in that game. We were down 40 to 15, 25 points at the top of the second quarter, and by halftime, we were tied up 53 to 53. So I would say that right there was the point where we dug in, we started getting stops on the defensive end, and to outscore a team, especially a great offensive team like the Lakers, 40 to 13 for the rest of the second quarter says a lot.

clips.text: I think that's ridiculous. What people have to understand is it takes a month or two just for your legs to kind of kick in. I can still play. I know my beginning of the season, my numbers aren't going to be great, but I know once I get to December, January, end of January, my numbers are going to go up a little bit. It's a game of averages, and I think the averages are a way out. He's starting off slow right now, that's normal for James. He usually picks it up in the December, end of January, so I'm not too worried about that, not at all.

clips.pull_quote: I think that's ridiculous. What people have to understand is it takes a month or two.

clips.speaker: Patrick Beverley
clips.text: If we are being transparent, Philadelphia just lost to Cleveland and it's probably one of James Harden's best games. But what Cleveland is doing, the best player on the team is Tyrese Maxey. In my opinion, Tyrese Maxey has been the best player in Philadelphia probably for the last two or three years consistently because Joel Embiid has been out with injury here and there. When you have a young leader like that at the point guard position, how dynamic he is, and I don't think a lot of people understand how much he works on his game. Me being in that locker room, I was the first vet that he had that he became an All-Star that first year. He's the best player. You add a person with Jaylen Brown, you add VJ Edgecombe, you have Embiid obviously, you have LeBron James, I think that makes his opportunities that much better.

clips.pull_quote: Tyrese Maxey has been the best player in Philadelphia probably for the last two or three years.

clips.speaker: Patrick Beverley
clips.text: The first thing that jumps right off when you talk about anything with a team is the leader, and that has to go to Nick Nurse. We do a disservice to coaches throughout the year. Nick Nurse got these two juggernauts, LeBron James and Jaylen Brown, in free agency and his ability to not only put it together, and we see what's going on in Miami how it has to take time. His ability to demand so much from his players, and I've been around him as a player and under his coaching staff, his ability to put those pieces together seamlessly so fast is very impressive. To have his team, guys who we talk about LeBron James, arguably one, two spots to ever do it, Joel Embiid, arguably if healthy the best center ever do it, Jaylen Brown, Finals MVP, to have these guys sacrifice so much, I think that's the really impressive part.
clips.news_angle: Patrick Beverley credits Nick Nurse for the 76ers' team chemistry
clips.social_post: Patrick Beverley credits Nick Nurse for the 76ers team chemistry, praising his ability to get superstars like LeBron James, Joel Embiid, and Jaylen Brown to sacrifice for the team so quickly.
clips.video_title: Doc Rivers Disses Giannis? Pat Bev Weighs In On LeBron, Giannis, Harden & more
clips.pull_quote: The first thing that jumps right off when you talk about anything with a team is the leader.

clips.speaker: Patrick Beverley
clips.text: They are able to expedite the growth of their young players because of so many greats and veterans that they do have in the locker room. You have Al Horford who is still there, you have Draymond Green who is still there, you have Chris Paul, sorry, yep, he's not there anymore. We don't know what's going on with him. But you have these veterans that can expedite the mindset of these young players and that's what you see in the Warriors. I love his story. I love him working in the factory with his mom, just started playing basketball four or five years ago. I love his story, so you have a story like that put on a team like this, I think only good things happen.

clips.text: I'm probably one of my toughest covers. I think it's more of his IQ, and that's what you have to give a lot of credit to, his culture and the European mindset. He's not going to settle. It looks like he's settling a lot when he shoots the step-back threes, but that's just his go-to. If he knows something is working, he's going to continue to do that and do that over and over. He's probably, when it's all said and done, historically he probably would be the best player to play pick and roll when his career is over. When he's healthy, he's put up Michael Jordan numbers in the playoffs.

Luka Doncic's numbers in the playoffs are close to Michael Jordan. That's just the honest to God truth. His numbers are very, very similar to Michael Jordan. So I think it is, sometimes we do get lost on what we love and what we don't like, but as older people as we know, it's a new generation and we got to step out our box a little bit.

Now if your superstar players don't know how to sacrifice, you have to question the IQ of your players now. Maybe they didn't know, maybe I didn't teach you well, maybe they didn't understand it. clips.speaker: Sam Quinn
clips.text: The Thunder needed to do something. They addressed their 15th roster spot temporarily, they signed Dalen Terry, but this is more of a long-term move. We were both discussing, is there a guy on a rookie contract they could target, maybe like a Ryan Dunn, and they chose Nique Clifford, probably because of this really low price point. They have 2028 second-round picks. It's really nothing. And his salary is pretty low for a guy on a rookie scale. Less than what the Thunder are paying for other guys. Nique Clifford is going to make 3.3 million this year and 3.4 million the following year. So we'll see how he does this year if he can play enough this year. If and then like also the first month of next season will probably determine whether the Thunder pick up his option. So overall for the Thunder, it's fine, a fine addition. They needed to do something. I don't expect them to really be a regular part of the rotation, but then again, and as we'll really get into the discussion, this was more of a referendum on the Kings' process because I wouldn't be surprised if this, if he just ends up being an actual player as soon as he goes to the Thunder. Like as soon as the Thunder want to get one of your guys, that should automatically be some red flag that, hey, maybe you shouldn't do this trade.
clips.news_angle: Thunder's trade for Nique Clifford is a questionable move
clips.social_post: The Thunder adding Nique Clifford is a fine long term move for a low price point, but I do not expect him to be a regular part of the rotation this year.
clips.video_title: Nique Clifford Trade, Luka Raising the Lakers, Celtics Check, & Nuggets Convo | Third Apron Podcast
clips.pull_quote: Why do you keep giving up on your first round picks so quickly during their rookie deals?

clips.speaker: Sam Quinn
clips.text: You'd think the Kings would have learned their lesson, obviously with Tyrese Haliburton, but even on a more appropriate level for this trade, Davion Mitchell. Why do you keep giving up on your first round picks so quickly during their rookie deals? And the cost here is, it's one thing where Philly gave up on Jared McCain, who was the number 16 pick, and they got back a first round pick that was number 22. So it's like you're getting back roughly what you put in, you're liquidating. He didn't look good in the first half of last season, fine. I understood the downside for Philly at the time, but there was real reason to make that trade based on how badly he was playing. I understood wanting to cash out, I understood Daryl Morey's quote about selling high. The Kings aren't selling high. Nique Clifford played well for them last year down the stretch. It's easy to forget this because they were so bad, but they weren't tanking down the stretch last year. Nique Clifford was like one of the best players on their team in March and April. He averaged like 14, 5 and 4. He just barely plays for eight games and you're cashing him out in November, really, this early? I understand that you have Zach LaVine, you have Malik Monk, these guys who in the past you might not have played at all, but because of the new lottery rules, you want to put your veterans on the floor just for the relegation zone's sake. Fine, I get that.
clips.news_angle: Kings' trade of Nique Clifford is a bad organizational move
clips.social_post: The Kings giving up on Nique Clifford so quickly is a questionable organizational move. He played well down the stretch last year and they are not selling high here.

clips.text: Luka is pulling a James Harden in that he's leading the NBA in both three-point attempts and free-throw attempts, which sounds incongruous, but both Luka and Harden are doing it, or Luka is doing it and Harden did it. And doing it on an absurd 67% true shooting. So he's averaging 40 points per game. I have to imagine some of this stuff will come down a little bit, but either way the numbers are still going to be like very high. Like maybe doesn't finish with 40 points per game, but maybe 35, 36 could be in play. So he's just like unguardable at this level. Definitely the MVP front-runner at this point.

clips.pull_quote: Luka is pulling a James Harden in that he's leading the NBA in both three-point attempts and free-throw attempts.

clips.speaker: Sam Quinn
clips.text: It's interesting because you're right about the Lakers, now by virtue of the Thunder not being the Thunder, you have to take them a little bit more seriously. But at the same time, that's also true of the Rockets and the Timberwolves. So we've gone from this world where there were two superpowers in the West that were destined to play in the Western Conference Finals, to now one of those teams is still standing in San Antonio. And I'm kind of just watching how the bracket shakes out, because I think the Lakers, the Rockets, or the Timberwolves could challenge them in very different ways, but one of those teams is going to lose to one of the others in the second round, and the season is going to be looked at as a real disappointment. I am a little bit lower on the Lakers' start, like relative to the crazy, you know, 9-and-2 record, Luka averaging 40. I think what Luka is doing, like I think he's going to win MVP. I picked him before the season. I don't think he's going to keep averaging 40. The standout thing is the three-point shooting. It's how easy they look, right? It's the step-back 34-footer that just goes in like a layup, the confidence has never been more visible for him than it is now.

clips.speaker: Sam Quinn
clips.text: The West now, between Dallas and Portland and Golden State, the West is so deep that I think you can't reasonably expect to make it to the NBA Finals on the strength of one guy being this good. I think they're going to need a couple more things, but overall I have the same sentiment. I would still pick Houston, of a fully healthy Houston team, I probably still pick a fully Minnesota team, but I don't think these teams, I think they're all relatively still on the same tier. Oklahoma City, if they can maybe get one of those guys back, I would probably pick Oklahoma City over them. But the way Luka is playing, it's just, you got to just give him like a little bit of like a punter's chance.

That is like, if you would have told me to predict the five least likely things to happen this NBA season, that would have been on that list. These are the on-off splits rounded over the last six seasons for Nikola Jokic: plus 13, plus 21, plus 18, plus 21, plus 12, plus 17. That's just offense, that's not factoring in defense. For the Nuggets to be worse on offense with Nikola Jokic on the floor is one of the most absurd statistical things I have maybe ever seen in my entire time covering the NBA. It's only been a couple weeks, maybe that changes, but there are a lot of concerns here.

clips.text: People assume that it's all partying and jewelry and all these super expensive things, but in reality, it's just enjoying life on another level. clips.speaker: Dwight Powell
clips.team: UNDERSTAND THE GRIND WITH NORMAN POWELL
clips.text: You sacrifice family time, you sacrifice social time, and it starts at a very young age. You get used to being on your own, you get used to being misunderstood, you get used to being made fun of for being different or not doing what the social norm is, especially at a young age like going to parties, hanging out with your friends, wanting to be in the gym, wanting to workout.

clips.channel_team: UNDERSTAND THE GRIND WITH NORMAN POWELL
clips.pull_quote: You get used to being on your own, you get used to being misunderstood.

clips.speaker: Dwight Powell
clips.team: UNDERSTAND THE GRIND WITH NORMAN POWELL
clips.text: In college, being a young 18-year-old teenager, going off on my own to UCLA and being promised certain things from a coach, and then those things not happening and being pulled out of the starting lineup to come off the bench, and then you're looking at NBA draft and your draft stock as a teenager, and you go from first-round pick to late first, to early second, to late second, to not even being on the draft board, you kind of feel like your NBA dream is slipping away.

clips.social_post: Dwight Powell opens up about his time at UCLA, describing the mental toll of seeing his draft stock plummet from a first round pick to falling off the board entirely.
clips.video_title: What People Don't See Behind the NBA Lifestyle
clips.channel_team: UNDERSTAND THE GRIND WITH NORMAN POWELL
clips.pull_quote: Being a young 18-year-old teenager, going off on my own to UCLA and being promised certain things.

clips.speaker: Dwight Powell
clips.team: UNDERSTAND THE GRIND WITH NORMAN POWELL
clips.text: When you're a third-year player and even a fourth-year player, they feel like you reached your ceiling, which is kind of crazy to me because you're still 21, 22 years old. How I've been able to use every single obstacle as motivation and fuel to the fire to keep going, to keep working, to keep grinding. A lot of things that you go through that you've seen break other people or made other people quit or not want to push as hard or find an easier route, I stuck with it.

clips.social_post: Dwight Powell calls it crazy that teams decide a player has reached their ceiling by age 21 or 22. He says he used those obstacles as fuel to keep grinding.

clips.pull_quote: They feel like you reached your ceiling, which is kind of crazy to me.
